title: Cardiac Arrhythmias
subject: Medicine
summary: Arrhythmias are disturbances of heart rhythm that can be benign or life‑threatening. Recognising patterns, underlying causes and appropriate urgent actions is essential, especially where diagnostics are limited.

sections.p: An arrhythmia is any deviation from the normal sinus rhythm in rate, regularity, or conduction. Diagnosis is made by pulse assessment and ECG, looking for rate, rhythm, QRS width and axis.
b: Sinus rhythm: regular, rate 60‑100, P‑QRS‑T sequence
Bradycardia: <60 bpm, may be symptomatic
Tachycardia: >100 bpm, classify narrow vs wide QRS

sections.p: Severity is judged by haemodynamic impact and risk of degeneration to ventricular fibrillation.
b: Stable: normal blood pressure, no chest pain, no syncope
Unstable: hypotension, altered mental status, acute heart failure, chest pain
Life‑threatening: pulseless ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation

sections.p: Identify precipitating factors; in low‑resource settings infectious and metabolic triggers are common.
b: Electrolyte disturbances – hypokalaemia, hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia
Ischaemic heart disease – acute MI, chronic coronary disease
Infections – malaria, HIV‑related myocarditis, TB pericarditis
Drug‑induced – quinine, anti‑arrhythmics, herbal stimulants
Structural heart disease – rheumatic valve disease, cardiomyopathy, sickle‑cell cardiomyopathy

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or present with palpitations, dizziness, syncope, chest pain or heart failure signs.
b: Palpitations: awareness of irregular beats
Syncope/presyncope: sudden drop in cerebral perfusion
Dyspnoea: due to reduced cardiac output or heart failure
Chest discomfort: especially with ischaemic tachyarrhythmias

t.b: What rhythm is present and is there evidence of ischaemia or electrolyte effect?
Are electrolyte abnormalities contributing?
Is there myocardial injury driving the arrhythmia?
Is there evidence of heart enlargement, pulmonary oedema or TB?
Is there pericardial effusion or severe ventricular dysfunction?

sections.p: Prompt recognition of instability prevents sudden cardiac death.
b: Hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) with arrhythmia
Altered consciousness or seizures
Chest pain suggestive of acute MI
Signs of heart failure – pulmonary crackles, peripheral oedema

sections.p: Treat the precipitating cause, stabilise the patient, then apply rhythm‑specific therapy.
b: Immediate: oxygen, IV access, monitor, treat reversible causes (e.g., replace K+ if <3.3 mmol/L)
Tachyarrhythmias with instability → synchronized cardioversion (100 J for SVT, 200 J for VT)
Stable narrow‑complex SVT → vagal maneuvers, then adenosine if available; avoid beta‑blockers in acute asthma
Stable wide‑complex VT → amiodarone infusion; avoid class IC drugs in structural heart disease
Long‑term: beta‑blockers for rate control in AF, anticoagulation if CHA₂DS₂‑VASc ≥2, consider rhythm control if symptomatic

sections.p: Arrange outpatient review within 1 week for persistent arrhythmia or after discharge from an unstable episode.
b: Educate on avoiding stimulants, correcting electrolyte imbalance, and adherence to malaria prophylaxis or HIV therapy
Screen for underlying structural disease with echocardiography when feasible
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce cardiac stress

sections.p: Distinguish arrhythmias from other causes of palpitations or syncope.
b: Premature beats (PVCs/PACs) – isolated, usually benign
Anxiety‑related tachycardia – normal sinus rhythm, no ECG abnormalities
Orthostatic hypotension – drop in BP on standing, not rhythm disturbance

sections.p: Certain findings may mask the severity of an arrhythmia.
b: Normal potassium in a patient on diuretics may hide intracellular depletion; check Mg2+
A ‘normal’ ECG taken after a brief episode may miss paroxysmal AF; consider Holter or event monitor
Low‑grade fever can be misattributed to infection while the real trigger is electrolyte loss

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid wide‑complex tachycardia (>150 bpm) causing breathlessness

faq.q: Why is hypokalaemia dangerous in arrhythmias?
faq.a: Low K+ prolongs repolarisation, creating early after‑depolarisation and predisposes to ventricular tachycardia.

faq.q: When is cardioversion preferred over drugs?
faq.a: When the patient is haemodynamically unstable or when rapid restoration of sinus rhythm is needed.

faq.q: Can atrial fibrillation be managed without anticoagulation?
faq.a: Only if the CHA₂DS₂‑VASc score is 0 (men) or 1 (women); otherwise anticoagulation is required to prevent stroke.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with malaria presents with palpitations and a pulse of 130 bpm – what is your immediate assessment and why? — Check haemodynamic stability, obtain ECG, correct electrolytes; malaria can cause hypokalaemia precipitating SVT.

You see a regular wide‑complex tachycardia at 180 bpm in a patient with known rheumatic mitral stenosis – what is the most likely rhythm and next step? — Likely ventricular tachycardia; if unstable, immediate synchronized cardioversion.

A patient on quinine for severe malaria develops a new irregular pulse; ECG shows absent P waves and irregularly irregular QRS – what is the diagnosis and management? — New‑onset atrial fibrillation; control rate with digoxin (avoid beta‑blocker if bronchospasm) and assess anticoagulation need.
Why is adenosine contraindicated in a patient with asthma presenting with SVT? — Adenosine can cause bronchospasm; use vagal maneuvers or calcium channel blocker instead.

Explain how you would differentiate between a PVC and ventricular tachycardia on a limited ECG strip. — PVCs are isolated, have a compensatory pause; VT shows a series of wide QRS complexes without normal beats.

A child with sickle‑cell disease presents with sudden tachycardia and chest pain; ECG is normal. What non‑cardiac cause should you consider? — Acute pain crisis causing sympathetic surge; treat pain and reassess rhythm.
When is a trans‑cutaneous pacemaker indicated in bradyarrhythmia? — When symptomatic bradycardia persists despite atropine and the patient is unstable.

What electrolyte abnormality is most likely to cause a peaked T wave and how does it affect arrhythmia risk? — Hyperkalaemia (>5.5 mmol/L) shortens repolarisation, leading to peaked T waves and risk of ventricular fibrillation.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A detailed history is crucial to identify precipitating factors, assess symptom severity, and guide initial management. Physical examination focuses on signs of hemodynamic instability, underlying cardiac disease, and potential systemic causes of arrhythmia.
b: When did the symptoms start and how long do they last? (Onset, duration, frequency, and termination of episodes).
What are the associated symptoms? (Palpitations, dizziness, syncope, chest pain, shortness of breath, fatigue, weakness, anxiety).
Are there any aggravating or relieving factors? (Exercise, rest, stress, caffeine, alcohol, specific body positions).
What is the patient's past medical history? (Previous cardiac disease, hypertension, diabetes, thyroid disorders, chronic lung disease, renal or liver impairment, HIV, TB, malnutrition).
What medications is the patient currently taking? (Prescription, over-the-counter, herbal remedies, illicit drugs, especially anti-arrhythmics, quinine, tricyclic antidepressants).
Is there a family history of sudden cardiac death or arrhythmias?
General appearance: Assess for signs of distress, pallor, cyanosis, or diaphoresis, which may indicate poor perfusion or severe illness.
Vital signs: Measure blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation. Note any hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg), bradycardia (<60 bpm), or tachycardia (>100 bpm).
Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP): Observe for elevated JVP, which can indicate right heart failure or fluid overload. Look for cannon A waves, which suggest AV dissociation (e.g., in VT).

Palpation of pulses: Palpate radial and femoral pulses simultaneously to assess rate, rhythm, and character. Note any pulse deficit (difference between apical and radial pulse rate, common in atrial fibrillation).

Cardiac auscultation: Listen for heart sounds (S1, S2), murmurs (suggesting valvular heart disease like rheumatic mitral stenosis), gallop rhythms (S3, S4 indicating heart failure), and pericardial rubs (pericarditis).
Lung auscultation: Listen for crackles or wheezes, indicating pulmonary oedema (left heart failure) or bronchospasm (e.g., in severe asthma, which is a contraindication for adenosine).
Peripheral examination: Check for peripheral oedema (right heart failure), clubbing, or signs of peripheral embolization (e.g., in atrial fibrillation).

Neurological examination: Assess mental status for confusion or altered consciousness, which are signs of severe hemodynamic compromise. A bedside examination cannot definitively diagnose the specific type of arrhythmia or its underlying electrophysiological mechanism.

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm the diagnosis of arrhythmia, identify its type, assess its impact on cardiac function, and uncover underlying causes, especially those common in low-resource settings.

sections.p: Diagnosis of arrhythmia relies on ECG interpretation, while staging and severity assessment are based on hemodynamic stability and the risk of adverse outcomes. Prompt recognition of instability is critical.
b: Arrhythmia diagnosis: Any deviation from normal sinus rhythm in rate (bradycardia <60 bpm, tachycardia >100 bpm), regularity (regular, irregularly regular, irregularly irregular), or conduction (P-QRS-T sequence, PR interval, QRS width).
Sinus rhythm: Regular rhythm, rate 60-100 bpm, each QRS preceded by a P wave with a consistent PR interval (0.12-0.20 seconds), and a narrow QRS complex (<0.12 seconds).

Atrial Fibrillation (AF): Irregularly irregular rhythm, absence of distinct P waves, and chaotic atrial activity (fibrillatory waves) with an irregular ventricular response. This is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia in the adult population. Electrophysiological changes maintaining AF within a few hours of onset include atrial remodelling (electrical and structural),

Ventricular Tachycardia (VT): >3 consecutive PVCs at a rate typically between 100-250 bpm, with a wide QRS complex (>0.12 seconds) and often AV dissociation. Slower VTs (accelerated idioventricular rhythm) exist, and faster VTs can exceed 250 bpm.
Severity and Staging (based on hemodynamic impact):
Stable: Normal blood pressure (SBP >90 mmHg), no chest pain, no syncope, no altered mental status, no signs of acute heart failure. Patient is conscious and alert.

Unstable: Presence of one or more of the following: hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg), altered mental status or seizures, acute heart failure (pulmonary crackles, peripheral oedema), ongoing chest pain suggestive of acute myocardial ischaemia. Requires immediate intervention (e.g., synchronized cardioversion).

Life-threatening: Pulseless ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation. Requires immediate defibrillation and CPR. Altered mental status or seizures in the context of an arrhythmia indicate hemodynamic instability and require immediate assessment of pulse and rhythm, with synchronized cardioversion if a pulse is present with the arrhythmia.

sections.p: Several conditions can mimic or be confused with cardiac arrhythmias due to similar symptoms or ECG findings. Careful differentiation is essential for appropriate management.

sections.p: Management of arrhythmias follows a structured approach, prioritizing hemodynamic stability, identifying and treating underlying causes, and preventing recurrence. The choice of intervention depends on the type of arrhythmia, its impact on the patient, and available resources.
b: **First things first (Assess and Stabilize):** Immediately assess airway, breathing, and circulation (ABC). If the patient is unstable (hypotension, altered mental status, acute heart failure, chest pain), proceed to urgent synchronized cardioversion for tachyarrhythmias with a pulse, or defibrillation for pulseless ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation. Ensure IV access and att

**Identify and Treat Underlying Causes:** Address reversible factors such as electrolyte imbalances (e.g., potassium, magnesium), hypoxia, acidosis, hypothermia, and drug toxicities. In low-resource settings, consider infections like malaria or HIV-related myocarditis, and nutritional deficiencies, especially in refeeding syndrome.

**Bradyarrhythmias (Symptomatic):** If symptomatic (e.g., syncope, dizziness, hypotension), administer atropine intravenously. If atropine is ineffective, consider transcutaneous pacing. Isoprenaline or dopamine infusions may be used as temporary measures while awaiting definitive pacing.

**Narrow Complex Tachycardias (SVT):** For stable patients, attempt vagal maneuvers (e.g., Valsalva, carotid sinus massage). If unsuccessful, administer adenosine intravenously (rapid push followed by saline flush); avoid in severe asthma due to bronchospasm risk. If adenosine is contraindicated or ineffective, consider calcium channel blockers (e.g., verapamil, diltiazem) or b

**Wide Complex Tachycardias (VT/SVT with aberrancy):** If stable, and VT is suspected, administer antiarrhythmics such as procainamide, sotalol, or amiodarone intravenously. If uncertain between VT and SVT with aberrancy, treat as VT. If unstable, immediate synchronized cardioversion is indicated.

**Atrial Fibrillation/Flutter:** For rate control in stable patients, use beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol) or calcium channel blockers (e.g., diltiazem, verapamil). For rhythm control, consider antiarrhythmics like amiodarone, flecainide, or propafenone, or electrical cardioversion. Anticoagulation is crucial to prevent thromboembolism, guided by CHA2DS2-VASc score.

**Monitoring and Escalation:** Continuously monitor ECG, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation. If the patient's condition deteriorates or initial treatments are ineffective, escalate care to a higher level or refer to a specialist. Prepare for advanced life support interventions.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Antiarrhythmic drugs have specific mechanisms of action, but also a range of adverse effects and interactions that clinicians must be aware of to ensure patient safety and optimize treatment outcomes.
b: **Adenosine:** Causes transient flushing, dyspnoea, and chest discomfort due to its vasodilatory and bronchoconstrictive effects. It is contraindicated in severe asthma due to the risk of severe bronchospasm. Administer rapidly via IV push followed by a saline flush.

**Amiodarone:** Can cause significant long-term side effects affecting multiple organs, including pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyperthyroidism), liver enzyme elevation, corneal microdeposits, and photosensitivity. Renal impairment typically does not necessitate dose adjustment for amiodarone itself, as it is primarily hepatically metabolized. Monitor thyroi

**Beta-blockers (e.g., Metoprolol, Propranolol):** Can cause bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm (especially in asthma), and exacerbate heart failure. Use with caution in patients with reactive airway disease or decompensated heart failure. Monitor heart rate and blood pressure.

**Calcium Channel Blockers (e.g., Verapamil, Diltiazem):** Can cause bradycardia, hypotension, and constipation. Avoid in patients with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome and atrial fibrillation/flutter, as they can accelerate ventricular response. Monitor heart rate and blood pressure.

**Digoxin:** Has a narrow therapeutic window and can cause toxicity, especially with hypokalaemia or renal impairment. Symptoms of toxicity include nausea, vomiting, visual disturbances (yellow-green halos), and various arrhythmias (e.g., AV block, ventricular ectopy). Monitor serum digoxin levels and electrolytes.

**Procainamide:** Can cause hypotension, especially with rapid infusion, and can prolong the QT interval, increasing the risk of Torsades de Pointes. Long-term use can lead to a lupus-like syndrome. Monitor ECG for QT prolongation and blood pressure during administration.

sections.p: Arrhythmias can lead to severe complications if not promptly recognized and managed. Escalation of care is crucial when signs of instability or life-threatening conditions emerge.
b: **Hemodynamic Instability:** Hypotension (systolic BP <90 mmHg), altered mental status, acute heart failure (pulmonary oedema, crackles, peripheral oedema), or ongoing chest pain suggestive of myocardial ischaemia are immediate indications for escalation. This often requires urgent synchronized cardioversion or defibrillation.

**Cardiac Arrest:** Pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation are life-threatening emergencies requiring immediate defibrillation and advanced cardiac life support protocols. Asystole and pulseless electrical activity also require immediate resuscitation.

**Thromboembolism:** Atrial fibrillation significantly increases the risk of stroke and systemic embolization due to blood stasis in the left atrial appendage. Escalation involves prompt initiation of anticoagulation, unless contraindicated, and consideration of rhythm control strategies.

**Heart Failure Exacerbation:** Sustained tachyarrhythmias or severe bradyarrhythmias can reduce cardiac output, leading to or worsening heart failure. Signs include increasing dyspnoea, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, and worsening peripheral oedema. Management requires addressing the arrhythmia and optimizing heart failure treatment.

**Myocardial Ischaemia/Infarction:** Tachyarrhythmias can increase myocardial oxygen demand, leading to ischaemia, especially in patients with underlying coronary artery disease. New or worsening chest pain, ECG changes (ST depression/elevation), or elevated cardiac biomarkers warrant immediate investigation and management for acute coronary syndrome.

**Refractory Arrhythmia:** If an arrhythmia does not respond to initial medical or electrical therapies, or if it recurs frequently, it indicates a need for specialist consultation (cardiologist/electrophysiologist) for advanced management options such as catheter ablation or implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) placement.

sections.p: Various patient characteristics and comorbidities can significantly influence the presentation, diagnosis, and management of arrhythmias, particularly in low-resource settings.
b: **HIV:** HIV infection can directly affect the myocardium (HIV-associated cardiomyopathy) or lead to myocarditis, increasing the risk of arrhythmias. Opportunistic infections and antiretroviral drugs can also contribute. ECG changes may be subtle, and a high index of suspicion is needed.

**TB:** Tuberculous pericarditis can cause effusions and constrictive pericarditis, leading to arrhythmias, particularly atrial fibrillation. Antitubercular drugs can also have cardiac side effects. Diagnosis may be delayed due to non-specific symptoms.

**Malnutrition/Refeeding Syndrome:** Severe malnutrition, followed by rapid refeeding, can precipitate severe electrolyte imbalances (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia) and fluid shifts, leading to life-threatening arrhythmias, especially ventricular arrhythmias. Careful electrolyte monitoring and gradual refeeding are crucial.

**Pregnancy:** Hormonal changes, increased blood volume, and cardiac output can predispose pregnant women to arrhythmias. Management requires careful consideration of fetal safety, often preferring non-pharmacological approaches or drugs with established safety profiles (e.g., beta-blockers, adenosine). Cardioversion is generally safe if needed.

**Diabetes Mellitus:** Diabetic autonomic neuropathy can affect heart rate variability and predispose to arrhythmias. Diabetic cardiomyopathy also increases risk. Glycaemic control is important, and some antiarrhythmics may interact with hypoglycaemic agents.

**Drugs and Herbal Remedies:** Many medications (e.g., quinine for malaria, tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics) and traditional herbal remedies can prolong the QT interval or have direct arrhythmogenic effects. A detailed drug history, including over-the-counter and herbal preparations, is essential.

**Alcohol:** Acute alcohol intoxication can trigger 'holiday heart' syndrome (atrial fibrillation). Chronic alcohol abuse can lead to alcoholic cardiomyopathy, increasing the risk of various arrhythmias. Abstinence is key to management.

**Kidney or Liver Failure:** Impaired renal or hepatic function can alter drug metabolism and excretion, necessitating dose adjustments for many antiarrhythmics (e.g., digoxin, sotalol). Electrolyte imbalances (hyperkalaemia in renal failure) are also common and arrhythmogenic.

sections.p: The approach to arrhythmias varies significantly across different patient populations, requiring tailored strategies that account for unique physiological, pathological, and resource considerations.
b: **Children:** Arrhythmias in children are often congenital or related to structural heart disease. Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is the most common symptomatic arrhythmia. Management often starts with vagal maneuvers; adenosine is used with caution due to smaller body size. Irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves and chaotic ventricular response in a child is most

**Pregnancy:** As discussed, management prioritizes fetal safety. Vagal maneuvers are first-line for SVT. Beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol) are generally considered safe. Amiodarone is typically avoided due to fetal thyroid effects. Electrical cardioversion is safe and effective when indicated for unstable tachyarrhythmias.

**The Elderly:** Elderly patients often have multiple comorbidities (e.g., ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, renal impairment) and polypharmacy, increasing the risk of arrhythmias and adverse drug reactions. Doses of antiarrhythmics may need to be reduced. Atrial fibrillation is highly prevalent and anticoagulation is critical.

**People with HIV:** HIV-associated cardiomyopathy and myocarditis increase arrhythmia risk. Drug-drug interactions between antiretrovirals and antiarrhythmics are common and must be carefully managed. Close monitoring for electrolyte disturbances and cardiac side effects of medications is essential.

**Low-Resource Settings:** Diagnosis relies heavily on clinical assessment and basic ECG. Advanced investigations (e.g., electrophysiology studies) and treatments (e.g., ablation, ICDs) may be unavailable. Emphasis is on treating reversible causes (e.g., malaria, electrolyte imbalances, malnutrition), using readily available and affordable drugs, and prompt recognition of insta

t.b: Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia in the adult population, with its prevalence increasing with age and comorbidities.

facts: Amiodarone: loading dose typically over 24 hours
Synchronized cardioversion: initial energy 50-100 J for narrow regular SVT
Unstable tachycardia: SBP <90 mmHg, altered mental status, acute heart failure, chest pain
Atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular rhythm, absent P waves
Re-entry circuit: common mechanism for tachyarrhythmias
CHA2DS2-VASc score: assesses stroke risk in AF

vivas.q: A 45-year-old woman severely malnourished after prolonged starvation is started on full calorie total parenteral nutrition. Within 48 hours she develops severe hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, and cardiac arrhythmias. What is the underlying mechanism?
vivas.a: This is characteristic of refeeding syndrome. Rapid reintroduction of carbohydrates stimulates insulin release, driving phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium into cells, leading to severe intracellular electrolyte shifts and depletion, which can precipitate cardiac arrhythmias.

vivas.q: A 60-year-old patient presents with signs of systemic embolization, having suffered a transient ischemic attack. Echocardiography shows severe left atrial dilation and stagnant blood flow within the left atrial appendage. What is the most likely underlying cardiac arrhythmia?
vivas.a: Atrial fibrillation is the most likely arrhythmia. Left atrial dilation and stagnant blood flow in the left atrial appendage are classic findings that promote thrombus formation, leading to systemic embolization, such as a TIA.

vivas.q: A patient undergoing rapid massive transfusion develops cardiac arrhythmia. Which factor is most likely contributing to this complication?
vivas.a: Citrate toxicity leading to hypocalcaemia is a common cause. Citrate in transfused blood products chelates calcium, and rapid transfusion can overwhelm the liver's ability to metabolize citrate, resulting in symptomatic hypocalcaemia and arrhythmias.

vivas.q: What is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia in the adult population?
vivas.a: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia in adults. Its prevalence increases with age and is associated with various cardiovascular risk factors.

vivas.q: What characteristic electrophysiological change occurs within a few hours of the onset of atrial fibrillation to maintain the arrhythmia?
vivas.a: Electrical remodeling occurs, characterized by shortening of the atrial refractory period and increased dispersion of refractoriness. This creates a substrate that facilitates the perpetuation of multiple re-entrant wavelets, maintaining the irregularly irregular rhythm.

vivas.q: A patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy develops atrial fibrillation. What is the primary reason for the development of arrhythmias in this condition?
vivas.a: Left atrial enlargement and increased left ventricular diastolic pressure due to impaired relaxation in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy lead to atrial stretch and fibrosis. This creates an arrhythmogenic substrate for re-entry and ectopic foci, predisposing to atrial fibrillation.

vivas.q: What is the defining electrocardiographic feature of a sinus arrhythmia?
vivas.a: Sinus arrhythmia is characterized by an irregular heart rate where the P-P interval varies by more than 0.12 seconds (120 ms or 3 small squares) with respiration, but each P wave is followed by a QRS complex and the P wave morphology is consistent.

vivas.q: An ECG on a child shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with an absence of clear P waves and chaotic ventricular response. Which arrhythmia is most consistent with this description?
vivas.a: This description is most consistent with atrial fibrillation. The irregularly irregular rhythm, absence of distinct P waves, and chaotic ventricular response are classic ECG features of atrial fibrillation.

vivas.q: List and explain the main features of Sinus Arrhythmia as described in the notes.
vivas.a: Sinus arrhythmia is a normal physiological variant. Its main features include: 1. Irregular heart rate, typically varying with respiration (rate increases with inspiration, decreases with expiration). 2. Normal P wave morphology preceding each QRS complex. 3. Normal PR interval. 4. Normal QRS duration and morphology. It is benign and requires no treatment.

vivas.q: Explain how conduction disorders can lead to reduced cardiac output.
vivas.a: Conduction disorders, such as severe bradyarrhythmias or tachyarrhythmias, disrupt the heart's pumping efficiency. Bradycardia reduces cardiac output by decreasing heart rate, while tachycardia can reduce diastolic filling time, leading to decreased stroke volume and thus reduced cardiac output.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate between a supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) with aberrancy and ventricular tachycardia (VT) on an ECG?
vivas.a: Key differentiating features include AV dissociation (P waves marching through QRS complexes independently) which strongly suggests VT, fusion beats and capture beats which are pathognomonic for VT, and specific QRS morphology criteria (e.g., Brugada criteria, Vereckei criteria). SVT with aberrancy typically has a QRS morphology resembling a bundle branch block.

vivas.q: What are the immediate management steps for a patient presenting with an unstable wide-complex tachycardia?
vivas.a: Immediate management for unstable wide-complex tachycardia is synchronized cardioversion. While preparing for cardioversion, ensure airway, breathing, and circulation are supported, gain IV access, and attach defibrillator pads.

vivas.q: When is adenosine contraindicated, and what are its common side effects?
vivas.a: Adenosine is contraindicated in severe asthma due to the risk of bronchospasm, and in second- or third-degree AV block without a pacemaker. Common side effects include transient flushing, chest discomfort, dyspnoea, and a brief period of asystole.

vivas.q: Describe the bedside assessment of a patient presenting with palpitations.
vivas.a: Bedside assessment includes: 1. History: onset, duration, frequency, associated symptoms (dizziness, chest pain, syncope), precipitating/relieving factors, drug history (including herbal remedies). 2. Examination: vital signs (BP, HR, RR, SpO2), palpate pulse (rate, rhythm, character), auscultate heart for murmurs, signs of heart failure (JVP, crackles, oedema), thyroid examination.

vivas.q: What are the common causes of arrhythmias in low-resource settings?
vivas.a: Common causes include electrolyte disturbances (e.g., hypokalaemia from diarrhoeal diseases, malnutrition), infections (malaria, HIV-related myocarditis, TB pericarditis), rheumatic heart disease, and drug-induced arrhythmias (e.g., quinine, herbal remedies).

vivas.q: How does hypokalaemia lead to arrhythmias?
vivas.a: Hypokalaemia increases myocardial excitability and prolongs repolarization, leading to increased automaticity and re-entry. ECG changes include prominent U waves, T wave flattening/inversion, and ST depression, predisposing to ventricular ectopy and potentially life-threatening arrhythmias like Torsades de Pointes.

vivas.q: What is the role of amiodarone in arrhythmia management, and what are its key side effects?
vivas.a: Amiodarone is a broad-spectrum antiarrhythmic used for both supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias, particularly in patients with structural heart disease. Key side effects include pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyperthyroidism), liver toxicity, corneal microdeposits, and photosensitivity.

vivas.q: When is a transcutaneous pacemaker indicated in bradyarrhythmia?
vivas.a: A transcutaneous pacemaker is indicated for symptomatic bradyarrhythmias (e.g., severe sinus bradycardia, high-grade AV block) causing haemodynamic instability (hypotension, altered mental status, acute heart failure, chest pain) when atropine is ineffective or contraindicated, as a bridge to transvenous pacing or definitive management.

mcqs.q: A 35-year-old pregnant woman presents with sudden onset palpitations and dizziness. ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 170 bpm. She is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate initial management?
mcqs.e: Vagal manoeuvres are the first-line treatment for stable narrow-complex tachycardias, including in pregnancy, as they are non-invasive and safe. If unsuccessful, adenosine can be considered with caution in pregnancy.

mcqs.q: A 70-year-old patient with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with an irregularly irregular rhythm, absent P waves, and a ventricular rate of 140 bpm. He is stable. Which medication should be avoided for rate control?
mcqs.e: Beta-blockers like metoprolol are relatively contraindicated in patients with severe COPD due to the risk of bronchospasm. Calcium channel blockers (diltiazem) or digoxin are preferred for rate control in AF with COPD.

mcqs.q: A patient with known rheumatic mitral stenosis develops a regular wide-complex tachycardia at 180 bpm. He is hypotensive and has chest pain. What is the immediate management?
mcqs.e: The patient has an unstable wide-complex tachycardia (hypotension, chest pain). Immediate synchronized cardioversion is indicated for haemodynamic instability.

mcqs.q: A 50-year-old man on quinine for severe malaria develops a new irregular pulse. ECG shows absent P waves and a ventricular rate of 110 bpm. What is the most likely arrhythmia?
mcqs.e: The description 'irregular pulse, absent P waves' is classic for atrial fibrillation. Quinine can prolong the QT interval but is not a direct cause of AF, however, severe malaria itself can precipitate AF.

mcqs.q: A child with sickle-cell disease presents with sudden tachycardia and chest pain; ECG is normal. What is the most important next step in management?
o: Assess for signs of acute chest syndrome and manage pain
mcqs.e: In a child with sickle cell disease presenting with tachycardia and chest pain, even with a normal ECG, acute chest syndrome must be ruled out and managed promptly, as it is a life-threatening complication. Pain management and oxygen are crucial.

mcqs.q: Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is most likely to cause peaked T waves and how does it affect arrhythmia risk?
o: Hypokalaemia; increases risk of Torsades de Pointes
Hypocalcaemia; increases risk of QT prolongation
Hyperkalaemia; increases risk of ventricular fibrillation
mcqs.e: Hyperkalaemia causes peaked T waves, followed by QRS widening and eventually sine wave patterns. It increases the risk of severe bradyarrhythmias and ventricular fibrillation due to altered myocardial excitability.

cases.v: A 55-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diabetes presents to the emergency department complaining of sudden onset of 'racing heart' and shortness of breath for the past 2 hours. On examination, his pulse is 160 bpm and irregularly irregular. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, and he has fine crackles at both lung bases. An ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with no discernible P waves and a narrow QRS complex.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: The most likely diagnosis is Atrial Fibrillation with Rapid Ventricular Response (AFRVR), given the irregularly irregular rhythm, absent P waves, narrow QRS, and associated symptoms of shortness of breath and crackles.

qs.q: What long-term management considerations are important for this patient?
qs.a: Long-term management involves: 1. Rate control (if rhythm control is not pursued or failed). 2. Anticoagulation for stroke prevention based on CHA2DS2-VASc score (this patient likely scores high due to age, hypertension, diabetes). 3. Addressing underlying comorbidities like hypertension and diabetes. 4. Education on symptoms and adherence to medication.

cases.v: A 28-year-old woman, 30 weeks pregnant, presents with sudden onset severe dizziness and near-syncope. Her pulse is 200 bpm and regular. Her blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg. An ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia.

qs.q: What is the most likely arrhythmia and what is the immediate priority?
qs.a: The most likely arrhythmia is Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT). The immediate priority is to stabilize the patient due to haemodynamic instability (severe dizziness, near-syncope, hypotension).

qs.q: What is the immediate management for this patient?
qs.a: Given the haemodynamic instability, immediate synchronized cardioversion is indicated. While preparing for cardioversion, vagal manoeuvres can be attempted if time permits, but cardioversion should not be delayed. Fetal monitoring should be initiated if available.

qs.q: Are there any special considerations for managing this patient due to her pregnancy?
qs.a: Yes, special considerations include: 1. Fetal monitoring during cardioversion. 2. Avoiding drugs that may harm the fetus (e.g., some antiarrhythmics). Adenosine is generally considered safe in pregnancy if vagal manoeuvres fail and the patient is stable enough to attempt pharmacological conversion. 3. Positioning the patient in a left lateral decubitus position to avoid aortocaval compression.

mistakes: Confusing haemodynamic instability (hypotension, altered mental status, acute heart failure, chest pain) with pulseless VT/VF. Instability requires immediate synchronized cardioversion if a pulse is present.
Using adenosine in patients with severe asthma without considering the risk of bronchospasm. Adenosine is contraindicated in severe asthma.
Failing to recognize refeeding syndrome as a cause of arrhythmias in malnourished patients undergoing nutritional support.
Not initiating anticoagulation for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation based on risk scores (e.g., CHA2DS2-VASc) in stable patients.

Misinterpreting wide-complex tachycardia. Assuming all wide-complex tachycardias are VT without considering SVT with aberrancy, especially in stable patients where diagnostic maneuvers or specific ECG criteria are crucia
Delaying synchronized cardioversion in unstable tachyarrhythmias. Haemodynamic instability mandates immediate electrical cardioversion.
Overlooking electrolyte disturbances (especially potassium, magnesium, calcium) as common and treatable causes of arrhythmias, particularly in low-resource settings or critically ill patients.
Not considering underlying structural heart disease (e.g., rheumatic heart disease, cardiomyopathy) as a predisposing factor for arrhythmias in the East African context.
exam: A 45-year-old woman severely malnourished after prolonged starvation is started on full calorie total parenteral nutrition. Within 48 hours she develops severe hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, and cardiac arrhythmias. What is the underlying mechanism? — This is characteristic of refeeding syndrome. Rapid reintroduction of carbohydrates stimulates insulin release, driving phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium into cells, leading to severe intracellular electrolyte shifts and depletion, which can precipitate cardiac arrhythmias.

A 60-year-old patient presents with signs of systemic embolization, having suffered a transient ischemic attack. Echocardiography shows severe left atrial dilation and stagnant blood flow within the left atrial appendage. What is the most likely underlying cardiac arrhythmia? — Atrial fibrillation is the most likely arrhythmia. Left atrial dilation and stagnant blood flow in the left atrial appendage are classic findings that promote thrombus formation, leading to systemic embolization, such as a TIA.

A patient undergoing rapid massive transfusion develops cardiac arrhythmia. Which factor is most likely contributing to this complication? — Citrate toxicity leading to hypocalcaemia is a common cause. Citrate in transfused blood products chelates calcium, and rapid transfusion can overwhelm the liver's ability to metabolize citrate, resulting in symptomatic hypocalcaemia and arrhythmias.

What is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia in the adult population? — Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia in adults. Its prevalence increases with age and is associated with various cardiovascular risk factors.

What characteristic electrophysiological change occurs within a few hours of the onset of atrial fibrillation to maintain the arrhythmia? — Electrical remodeling occurs, characterized by shortening of the atrial refractory period and increased dispersion of refractoriness. This creates a substrate that facilitates the perpetuation of multiple re-entrant wavelets, maintaining the irregularly irregular rhythm.

A patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy develops atrial fibrillation. What is the primary reason for the development of arrhythmias in this condition? — Left atrial enlargement and increased left ventricular diastolic pressure due to impaired relaxation in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy lead to atrial stretch and fibrosis. This creates an arrhythmogenic substrate for re-entry and ectopic foci, predisposing to atrial fibrillation.

What is the defining electrocardiographic feature of a sinus arrhythmia? — Sinus arrhythmia is characterized by an irregular heart rate where the P-P interval varies by more than 0.12 seconds (120 ms or 3 small squares) with respiration, but each P wave is followed by a QRS complex and the P wave morphology is consistent.

An ECG on a child shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with an absence of clear P waves and chaotic ventricular response. Which arrhythmia is most consistent with this description? — This description is most consistent with atrial fibrillation. The irregularly irregular rhythm, absence of distinct P waves, and chaotic ventricular response are classic ECG features of atrial fibrillation.

List and explain the main features of Sinus Arrhythmia as described in the notes. — Sinus arrhythmia is a normal physiological variant. Its main features include: 1. Irregular heart rate, typically varying with respiration (rate increases with inspiration, decreases with expiration). 2. Normal P wave morphology preceding each QRS complex. 3. Normal PR interval. 4. Normal QRS duration and morphology. It is benign and requires no treatment.
